habitat: Small parties in dry grassland and open woodland.
summary: An uncommon resident. The upperparts are dark olive-brown, the head to the breast is grey, and there is a small white forehead. The eyes are yellow. The legs are dark brown or blackish. The white forehead sits forward of the eye, and the dark lower breast-band is usually narrow. In flight the underwings are black and white. The call is a piping thi-wit.

similar.note: Crowned Lapwing has a full white circle around a black cap and red legs. Senegal Lapwing has only a small white forehead and dark legs.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^11=2048 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 1024–4096.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

head.pattern: Small white forehead forward of the eye. Head to breast grey.

viewNotes.note: Grey head and breast, small white forehead and dark legs, in dry grassland.
White forehead forward of the eye, and the yellow eye.
The upperwing pattern is described as diagnostic, but the colours were not named in the text.
Black-and-white underwings, and a usually narrow dark breast-band.

calls.description: A piping thi-wit. The texts do not separate the sexes. Grade A from near Kateta, Uganda. The filename is Vanneau-terne, the French name. No playable grade A from South Africa outranked it.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman calls it an uncommon resident. Black-winged Lapwing is the comparison in Newman and is not on the Kruger list, so it is not linked. The call is grade A from Uganda. The stored Kemp name remains Lesser Blackwinged Plover.
